title: The factors that govern overruling, and what they actually constrain
bodyMd:
Common-law courts are bound by their own past decisions, but not absolutely: a precedent may be overruled. The doctrine that governs when this may happen is usually described as a balance. On one side stand the goods that flow from stability. Litigants can predict how disputes will be resolved; legislatures can draft against a settled background; and a court that changes its mind frequently invites the suspicion that its rulings track its membership rather than the law. On the other side stands the cost of perpetuating a decision that was wrong when it was made.

Courts have tried to make that balance tractable by listing factors. A precedent is more readily abandoned if its reasoning has been undermined by the court's own later decisions, if it has proved unworkable in practice, if the factual understandings it rested on have since changed, and if few people have arranged their affairs in reliance on it. The list has the look of an instrument for disciplining judgment, and it is commonly praised as one.

It disciplines less than it appears to, for two reasons. The first is that the factors are not commensurable and the list supplies no weights. A precedent may be badly unworkable and heavily relied upon at the same time, and nothing in the doctrine says which consideration should then prevail. The second and deeper difficulty is that most of the factors can be assessed only by someone who has already formed a view about whether the precedent was right. Unworkability is rarely a matter of administrative friction alone: a rule generates confusion in the lower courts largely when the judges applying it find the results it produces uncongenial. Whether reliance is legitimate is a judgment about which expectations the law ought to protect, and that is the very question the precedent purported to settle.

The conclusion to draw is not that the doctrine is empty. A court that must march through the factors is obliged to say, in public and in terms that can later be quoted back at it, why this precedent and not others should fall. That is a genuine constraint, but it is a constraint of candour rather than of outcome. The doctrine does not tell a court what to decide; it tells the court what it must be willing to argue.
accessibilityText: A four-paragraph prose passage about the common-law doctrine governing when a court may overrule its own precedent. The first paragraph sets out the balance between the benefits of stability and the cost of perpetuating a wrong decision. The second lists the factors courts use: whether the precedent's reasoning has been undermined by later decisions, whether it has proved unworkable, whether the factual understandings behind it have changed, and how heavily it has been relied upon. The third gives two reasons the list disciplines judgment less than it appears to: the factors carry no weights, and most of them can be assessed only by someone who already has a view about whether the precedent was correct. The fourth concludes that the doctrine imposes a constraint of candour rather than of outcome. No figures, tables or mathematical notation appear.

provenance.notes: Written from scratch for this item bank. Not adapted from, and not a paraphrase of, any LSAC passage, judicial opinion or published article. The factors described (undermined reasoning, unworkability, changed factual understandings, reliance) are general textbook categories of common-law precedent doctrine; no court, case or commentator is named, nothing is presented as a quotation, and the argument of paragraphs three and four, together with every sentence, is the author's own.
